source.title: Accidental Vulnerability: Factors in Fine-Tuning That Shift Model Safeguards
source.authors: Punya Syon Pandey; Samuel Simko; Kellin Pelrine; Zhijing Jin

record.file_problem: The full paper text is present. Some figure/table text is garbled, but the reported numerical tables relevant to the findings below are readable.
record.tranche_reason: It fine-tunes aligned chat models on harmful and benign/domain-specific datasets and measures harmful-response attack success, using a different LoRA setup and evaluation protocol from the original work.
record.gate_note: The paper reports ASRs for multiple fine-tuning datasets under GCG, AutoPrompt and PEZ, direct-prompt ASRs, and PEZ cross-model results. These are included below. It also reports category-specific attack results, checkpoint attacks, benchmark scores, persona measures and representation/LoRA statistics; these do not measure the specified claim versions closely enough to include as rows. LoRA norm shifts do not test whether a small set of weights carries safety. The paper does not measure aligned-vs-base per-token KL, compliant-opening prefills, decoding changes, or deepening safety training.
record.test_reason: LoRA-fine-tunes safety-trained chat models (mainly LLaMA 3.1 8B Instruct) on harmful, benign (Alpaca) and domain datasets. It measures harmful-response ASR with the HarmBench classifier, both on direct prompts and under GCG, AutoPrompt and PEZ. These are V1 and V2 tests by a different method from the originals.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly right, but incomplete. The authors argue that vulnerability after fine-tuning stems partly from dataset properties, not only attacks. Correlation and causal mediation via representation drift point to prompt toxicity, length, sentiment and lexical diversity. They say capabilities are preserved and that dataset screening should be part of the pipeline. Their wording that domain datasets show increased vulnerability rests on gains of 0–5 points.
record.recipe_differences: Uses LoRA fine-tuning of LLaMA 3.1 8B Instruct on Alpaca, domain-specific, and harmful datasets; measures direct and jailbreak ASRs with HarmBench and JailbreakV-28k, including GCG, AutoPrompt and PEZ. It does not report refusal-removal rates using the original study's exact evaluation recipe.
record.method_sensitivity: Outcome varies by dataset and attack method; PEZ ASR does not increase for benign or engineering fine-tuning on LLaMA 3.1, while GCG and AutoPrompt do. Direct ASRs also vary by prompt set. Cross-model PEZ values differ between Qwen 2.5 7B and Falcon 7B.

fits_no_version.finding: Causal mediation over dataset features: prompt toxicity (indirect effect 0.82) and response toxicity (direct effect 0.84) relate to ASR, mediated by representation drift; response type-token ratio (TTR) has a negative mediated effect. Table 7 has n=6 datasets.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Fine-tuning data features (toxicity, lexical diversity, length) predict how much safety degrades after fine-tuning.

fits_no_version.finding: LoRA Frobenius norms grow most for the harmful datasets, especially layers 17, 24 and 31 (Fig. 8, Table 23).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Harmful fine-tuning produces larger, layer-concentrated weight updates than benign fine-tuning (no causal safety test).

record.peer_reviewed: Proceedings of the International Association for Safe and Ethical Artificial Intelligence (IASEAI’26)
record.problems: No uncertainty estimates are given for the ASR results. The main reported fine-tuning evaluation uses one primary model; cross-model evaluation uses only PEZ. The harmful datasets contain thousands of samples rather than a few hundred. The paper reports ASR rather than a direct refusal rate, and attack ASR depends on the attack method and prompt set.
record.rows_left_out: Omitted category-specific ASRs from Figure 2 and Tables 14–16, checkpoint embedding ASRs from Table 21, and persona/general-capability metrics because they are either attack-category breakdowns, attack-method optimization measures, or not direct tests of the claim versions. Table 17 cross-model domain values are partly recorded in flattened grouped rows where separate dataset-to-number assignment is ambiguous in the extracted layout.

untested.parts: Few to few-hundred example regime (the harmful sets are about 4.9k examples); full-parameter fine-tuning; models other than LLaMA under direct prompts.
Carefully selected benign subsets; direct-prompt ASR on Qwen and Falcon.
Entire version: no per-position aligned-vs-base KL.
Entire version. Suffix attacks are used only as fixed probes, with no matched no-attack comparison; no prefilling or decoding changes.
Entire version: LoRA norms are measured, but there is no ablation or localization test.

missing.what: Falcon 7B Instruct PEZ ASR after LAT Harmful (38.8) and CB Harmful (52.5), against baseline 21.3
Corrected Qwen PEZ values: Benign 24.0, Engineering 23.3, Legal 23.5, Cybersecurity 23.5

record.verdict_notes: The attack-ASR prompt set is about 80 HarmBench prompts, inferred from the Tables 30–34 categories. Attacks use Best-of-N with N=5. No uncertainty is reported, so 1–5 point shifts are a few prompts each. LoRA rank 16 with early stopping at loss 1.3 may give light training, especially for the 52k-example Alpaca set. The reader's V4 'supports' label is removed: no row compares attacked with unattacked responses on the same prompts. The study is not an original source.

versions.untested_parts: Tests harmful-dataset fine-tuning with direct and jailbreak ASR measures, but does not establish that a few to a few hundred examples remove refusal almost entirely; reported harmful training datasets contain 4,948 and 4,994 samples.
Tests Alpaca and domain-specific fine-tuning with direct and jailbreak ASR measures; does not test carefully selected benign subsets as such.
No aligned/base per-token KL by response position is reported.
Tests GCG, AutoPrompt, and PEZ attacks, but not compliant-opening prefills or decoding changes.
LoRA norms are measured, but no weights or ranks are ablated or edited to test whether a small parameter set carries safety.
Dataset features and representation drift are examined, but not as causes of first-token concentration or safety shallowness.
No training method intended to deepen safety is evaluated.

relationships.condition: LoRA fine-tuning on LAT or CB harmful data (about 4.9k examples); LLaMA 3.1 8B under direct and attack prompts; Qwen 2.5 7B and Falcon 7B under PEZ
relationships.reason: Direct ASR rises 17 to 57–62 (HarmBench) and 15 to 62–72 (JailbreakV). Attack ASR roughly doubles or triples (r8, r9, r14, r15, r20, r21, r32–r35, r40, r47, r48).
relationships.display_finding: Direct attack success rose from 17 to 57–62 on HarmBench and from 15 to 62–72 on JailbreakV. Attack success under attack prompts roughly doubled or tripled.
